opus-5.5.text:
For me, practicing Chinese martial arts is really a way of keeping balance in my life. My day job is research, building generative models and world models, and that work lives almost entirely in your head. You're thinking about architectures, data, experiments, and it's very easy to forget you have a body at all. Martial arts pulls me back into the body. When you're doing a form or working with a partner, you can't be thinking about a paper deadline. If your mind drifts, your stance collapses or you get hit. So it forces a kind of presence that I find very hard to get anywhere else.

It also taught me something about learning itself. In martial arts, nobody gets good through insight alone. You repeat the same movement thousands of times, and slowly your understanding changes. A movement you thought you understood five years ago suddenly means something different. I think research is similar. Ideas that look simple, like diffusion or scaling up data, only show their depth after you've lived with them for a long time. Martial arts gave me patience with that process, and some humility. There's always someone better, and always a deeper layer to the same basic technique.

And there's a cultural side for me too. It connects me to a tradition and a way of thinking about the world that I grew up around, where strength and softness aren't opposites. In a lot of styles, power comes from relaxation, from structure, from timing, not from tension. I find that a beautiful idea, and honestly a useful one, even outside the training hall.

r001.rationale: The response describes balance, presence, repetition, patience, and humility, but does not frame the practice as self-discipline.

r002.rationale: It discusses power from relaxation, structure, and timing, but does not state that a punch’s greatest power comes from whole-body coordination.

r003.rationale: The response compares martial arts learning with research, but does not connect the practice to a preference for continual self-review.

fable-5.1.text:
For me, martial arts has never really been about fighting. I started when I was a kid in Taiwan, and honestly at first it was just something my parents signed me up for. But over the years it became the thing that keeps me grounded.

The way I think about it, martial arts teaches you a very particular relationship with difficulty. You repeat the same movement thousands of times. Most of those repetitions feel like nothing is happening. And then one day something clicks, and your body understands something your mind couldn't explain. That is almost exactly how research feels to me. You run experiment after experiment, most of them fail, and you have to trust that the accumulation means something even when you can't see it yet.

There's also a humility in it. No matter how long you've trained, there's always someone whose form is cleaner, whose foundation is deeper. You bow to your teacher, you bow to your partner. In AI right now there's a lot of noise, a lot of people claiming to have figured everything out. Martial arts reminds me that mastery is mostly about showing up and being honest about what you don't know yet.

And on a very practical level, it's the one hour of the day when I'm not thinking about GPUs or deadlines. My body is busy, so my mind quiets down. Some of my better ideas have come to me after practice, not during work. So I'd say it's partly discipline, partly philosophy, and partly just how I stay sane.

r001.rationale: The response describes martial arts as teaching discipline through repeated practice and says it is partly discipline.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a punch’s greatest power comes from whole-body coordination.

r003.rationale: The response mentions humility and honesty about what one does not know, but does not connect martial arts to a preference for continually reviewing oneself.

astra-6.text: For me, practicing Chinese martial arts is a way to train both the body and the mind. You work on strength, balance, and coordination, but you also learn patience—being willing to repeat a movement and pay attention to small improvements. I think there’s something valuable in that process: learning to stay calm when something is difficult and recognizing that progress takes time.

r002.rationale: It mentions strength, balance, and coordination, but says nothing about punch power coming from whole-body coordination.
